God's care for his people (verses 1–9)

Could any pagan god raise up a person in righteousness, direct that person as he chose, and grant victories over nations?

The Lord did this with Abraham—or, as Henry considers more likely in this prophecy, would do so with Cyrus.

Sinners encourage one another along paths of wrongdoing. Should not those serving the living God encourage one another still more actively in his service?

God's people are descendants of Abraham, his friend. Henry calls this the highest title ever given to a human being. Through divine grace Abraham became like God in character and was admitted to fellowship with him.

Happy are the Lord's servants who have been called his friends, to walk with him in faith and holy obedience.

Such favored people need not give way to fear. The conflict may be intense, but the victory is certain.

The Lord strengthens those who must not fear (verses 10–20)

God speaks tenderly: Do not fear, for I am with you.

He is not merely near enough to be called; he is present.

Are you weak? He will strengthen you. Do you lack friends? He will help when you need help. Are you about to fall? His righteous right hand will uphold you, rewarding good and judging evil.

Some seek the ruin of God's people. But believers should not repay evil with evil. They must wait for the Lord's time.

Jacob is called a worm: weak, small, despised and readily trampled upon. God's people are worms in their humble opinion of themselves and in their enemies' proud opinion of them—but not vipers, belonging to the serpent's offspring.

God's word humbles human pride. Yet the Lord helps his people because he is their Redeemer.

He promises to turn Jacob into a new and sharp threshing instrument, prepared for useful work. Henry sees its fulfillment in the triumph of Christ's gospel and of faithful Christians over the powers of darkness.

God has prepared enough comfort to meet his people's needs and answer their prayers.

Our journey to heaven passes through the wilderness of this world. Human souls thirst for satisfaction, and grow weary of seeking in the world what the world cannot give.

Yet God promises refreshment even where no one expects it: rivers of grace and living water. Christ used living water as a figure of the Holy Spirit (John 7:38–39).

When God establishes his church in the wilderness of the Gentile world, the change will be like thornbushes turning into cedars, firs and myrtles.

These gifts are for the poor in spirit who hunger for divine light, forgiveness and holiness. God's Spirit makes barren hearts fruitful so others can recognize his work.

Idols cannot foretell or save (verses 21–29)

Often the quickest way to expose the folly of sin is to examine the reasons people give for defending it.

There is nothing in idols deserving our trust. They are worse than worthless.

Let those who offer doctrines other than salvation through Christ present their case. Can they provide a cure for the corruption of human nature?

Only Jehovah possesses irresistible power and certain knowledge of what lies ahead. He reveals his plans and fulfills them.

Henry contrasts biblical prophecy with all other predictions, which he regards as uncertain.

The return of captives from Babylon displayed God's power. But in the redemption accomplished by Christ, he revealed something far greater.

The gospel's good news—long hidden from previous ages—announces a Deliverer more glorious and powerful than the one who rescued the captive Jews.

May we belong among his obedient servants and faithful friends.

Verses 1-9 Can any heathen god raise up one in righteousness, make what use of him he pleases, and make him victorious over the nations? The Lord did so with Abraham, or rather, he would do so with Cyrus. Sinners encourage one another in the ways of sin; shall not the servants of the living God stir up one another in his service? God's people are the seed of Abraham his friend. This is certainly the highest title ever given to a mortal. It means that Abraham, by Divine grace, was made like to God, and that he was admitted to communion with Him. Happy are the servants of the Lord, whom he has called to be his friends, and to walk with him in faith and holy obedience. Let not such as have thus been favoured yield to fear; for the contest may be sharp, but the victory shall be sure.
[Isa.41.10-Isa.41.20]
Verses 10-20 God speaks with tenderness; Fear thou not, for I am with thee: not only within call, but present with thee. Art thou weak? I will strengthen thee. Art thou in want of friends? I will help thee in the time of need. Art thou ready to fall? I will uphold thee with that right hand which is full of righteousness, dealing forth rewards and punishments. There are those that strive with God's people, that seek their ruin. Let not God's people render evil for evil, but wait God's time. It is the worm Jacob; so little, so weak, so despised and trampled on by every body. God's people are as worms, in humble thoughts of themselves, and in their enemies' haughty thoughts of them; worms, but not vipers, not of the serpent's seed. Every part of God's word is calculated to humble man's pride, and to make him appear little in his own eyes. The Lord will help them, for he is their Redeemer. The Lord will make Jacob to become a threshing instrument. God will make him fit for use, new, and having sharp spikes. This has fulfilment in the triumphs of the gospel of Christ, and of all faithful followers of Christ, over the power of darkness. God has provided comforts to supply all their wants, and to answer all their prayers. Our way to heaven lies through the wilderness of this world. The soul of man is in want, and seeks for satisfaction; but becomes weary of seeking that in the world, which is not to be had in it. Yet they shall have a constant supply, where one would least expect it. I will open rivers of grace, rivers of living water, which Christ spake of the Spirit, John 7:38,39. When God sets up his church in the Gentile wilderness, there shall be a great change, as if thorns and briers were turned into cedars, and fir-trees, and myrtles. These blessings are kept for the poor in spirit, who long for Divine enlightening, pardon, and holiness. And God will render their barren souls fruitful in the grace of his Spirit, that all who behold may consider it.
[Isa.41.21-Isa.41.29]
Verses 21-29 There needs no more to show the folly of sin, than to bring to notice the reasons given in defence of it. There is nothing in idols worthy of regard. They are less than nothing, and worse than nothing. Let the advocates of other doctrines than that of salvation through Christ, bring their arguments. Can they tell of a cure for human depravity? Jehovah has power which cannot be withstood; this he will make appear. But the certain knowledge of the future must be only with Jehovah, who fulfils his own plans. All prophecies, except those of the Bible, have been uncertain. In the work of redemption the Lord showed himself much more than in the release of the Jews from Babylon. The good tidings the Lord will send in the gospel, is a mystery hid from ages and generations. A Deliverer is raised up for us, of nobler name and greater power than the deliverer of the captive Jews. May we be numbered among his obedient servants and faithful friends.

The gentle servant and his coming (verses 1–4)

This prophecy was fulfilled in Jesus Christ (Matthew 12:17).

Let us rest our souls upon him and rejoice in him. For his sake, the Father will be pleased with us.

The Holy Spirit not only came upon Christ but remained upon him without measure.

He bore patiently the contradiction and opposition of sinners.

His kingdom is spiritual. He did not arrive surrounded by earthly honors.

He treats people oppressed by doubts and fears with great tenderness.

Some are like a bruised reed. Others resemble a smoking wick newly lit, already in danger of going out.

He does not despise them or burden them with more service or suffering than they can bear.

Through many miracles and his resurrection, he fully demonstrated the truth of his holy teaching.

Through his gospel and grace he establishes principles in human minds that make people wise and just.

Distant nations will wait for and welcome his law and gospel.

If we want to make our calling and election sure and enjoy the Father's delight, we must look to Christ, listen to him, trust him and obey him.

The blessing of Christ's kingdom (verses 5–12)

Redemption restores human beings to the obedience owed to their Creator.

Christ is the light of the world.

By his grace he opens minds Satan has blinded and frees people from the bondage of sin.

The Lord has upheld his church in former times.

He now gives fresh promises, which will be fulfilled as certainly as the earlier promises were.

When Gentiles join the church, God receives glory both in them and through them.

Let us give the Creator what belongs to him, taking care never to serve created things more than the One who made them.

God's truth overcomes opposition (verses 13–17)

The Lord will reveal his power and glory.

His voice will cry out through the preaching of his word.

The gospel contains warnings as well as promises. Its warnings of judgment must be preached alongside its blessings, to awaken a sleeping world.

The Lord triumphs through the power of his Spirit.

Those who oppose and blaspheme the gospel will be silenced and brought to shame.

Obstacles to its advance will be removed.

For people blind by nature, God will show the path to life and happiness through Jesus Christ.

Where knowledge is weak, he will turn darkness into light. Where obedience is weak, he will make the path plain.

God guides the people whom he brings onto the right path, and will not abandon them.

This is prophetic language but also a promise that can encourage every believer.

The blindness and unfaithfulness of God's people (verses 18–25)

The people are called to pay attention and consider their true condition.

Many perish because they fail to notice what is clearly before them.

Their ruin comes not from a total lack of information but from carelessness.

God is pleased to make his own righteousness known.

Yet because of their sins, his people were stripped of their possessions. Henry connects this warning with the later destruction of the Jewish nation.

No one can resist or escape God's righteous anger.

Sin brings terrible harm because it provokes divine judgment.

People who refuse to be humbled by lesser judgments should expect greater ones.

How many professing Christians remain as spiritually blind as those who have never known the truth!

God delights to save sinners through Christ's righteousness, but also glorifies his justice in judging proud people who despise his mercy.

Because God once poured out judgment on a people he had specially favored, we should fear lest we, while a promise of entering his rest remains, fail to receive it.

To those who by nature were blind, God will show the way to life and happiness by Jesus Christ. They are weak in knowledge, but He will make darkness light. They are weak in duty, but their way shall be plain. Those whom God brings into the right way, he will guide in it. While the Lord is well-pleased in saving sinners through the righteousness of Christ he will also glorify his justice, by punishing all proud despisers. Seeing God has poured out his wrath on his once-favoured people, because of their sins, let us fear, lest a promise being left us of entering into his rest, any of us should be found to come short of it.

God's enduring love and protection (verses 1–7)

God's favor and good will toward his people provide abundant comfort to every believer.

Wherever there is a new creation, God himself has formed it.

All whom he has redeemed through his Son's blood he has set apart as his own.

When God is for us, what enemy should make us afraid?

What are all the lives and treasures of Egypt and Ethiopia when compared with Christ's blood?

True believers are precious in God's sight, and he delights in them.

Even when they pass through fire and water, they need not fear destruction while God remains with them.

He will uphold them and bring them through.

God will gather the faithful from every direction.

With such promises before them, they should put away anxious fear.

God's people testify against idols (verses 8–13)

The worshipers of idols are challenged to defend the objects in which they trust.

People who make idols and rely on them become like the idols themselves.

They retain human bodies and faculties, but abandon ordinary good sense.

By contrast, God's people know the power of his grace, the sweetness of his comfort, his kind Providence and the truth of his promises.

Every servant of God has a story to tell about what he has done within and for them.

Such testimony may encourage other people to recognize, believe and rejoice in his power, truth and love.

Deliverance from Babylon and the greater redemption (verses 14–21)

The prophet announces the coming rescue from Babylon.

Yet the words also point beyond that nearer deliverance.

Henry sees in them redemption through Christ, the conversion of the Gentiles and the recall of the Jews.

Everything God does to rescue sinners and bring believers to final glory is astonishing.

Yet all of it rests upon the greater wonder of love revealed in the redemption of humanity.

The Lord calls sinners to repentance (verses 22–28)

People who neglect prayer have grown weary of God.

The Master did not exhaust his servants through harsh demands; they wearied him through their repeated disobedience.

Still his mercy remains extraordinary:

He himself blots out transgressions.

This gives sinners courage to repent, because there is forgiveness with God.

Forgiveness is a completely free act of divine mercy.

When God forgives, he no longer holds the pardoned sins against us.

He does not do so because we deserve forgiveness.

He pardons for his own mercy, according to his promise, and above all for his Son's sake.

To forgive in this way is his glory.

Can human beings justify themselves before him?

That attempt is hopeless. Our first father violated God's covenant, and all of us have followed his example.

We can expect pardon only by faith in Christ, accompanied by genuine repentance and followed by newness of life, hatred of sin and love for God.

Let us remind the Lord of the promises he has made to repentant sinners and of the satisfaction his Son has made for them.

Bring those promises before him in earnest prayer for forgiveness.

This is the sure way to be justified freely by his grace and to find peace.

What are Egypt and Ethiopia, all their lives and treasures, compared with the blood of Christ? True believers are precious in God's sight, his delight is in them, above any people. Though they went as through fire and water, yet, while they had God with them, they need fear no evil; they should be born up, and brought out. The faithful are encouraged. [Isa.43.8-Isa.43.13]
Verses 8-13 Idolaters are called to appear in defence of their idols. Those who make them, and trust in them, are like unto them. They have the shape and faculties of men; but they have not common sense. But God's people know the power of his grace, the sweetness of his comforts, the kind care of his providence, and the truth of his promise. [Isa.43.14-Isa.43.21]
Verses 14-21 The deliverance from Babylon is foretold, but there is reference to greater events. The redemption of sinners by Christ, the conversion of the Gentiles, and the recall of the Jews, are described. All that is to be done to rescue sinners, and to bring the believer to glory, is little, compared with that wondrous work of love, the redemption of man.
[Isa.43.22-Isa.43.28]
Verses 22-28 Those who neglect to call upon God, are weary of him. The Master tired not the servants with his commands, but they tired him with disobedience. What were the riches of God's mercy toward them? I, even I, am he who yet blotteth out thy transgressions. This encourages us to repent, because there is forgiveness with God, and shows the freeness of Divine mercy. When God forgives, he forgets. It is not for any thing in us, but for his mercies' sake, his promise' sake; especially for his Son's sake. He is pleased to reckon it his honour. Would man justify himself before God? The attempt is desperate: our first father broke the covenant, and we all have copied his example. We have no reason to expect pardon, except we seek it by faith in Christ; and that is always attended by true repentance, and followed by newness of life, by hatred of sin, and love to God. Let us then put him in remembrance of the promises he has made to the penitent, and the satisfaction his Son has made for them. Plead these with him in wrestling for pardon; and declare these things, that thou mayest be justified freely by his grace. This is the only way, and it is a sure way to peace.

God's Spirit promised to his people (verses 1–8)

Israel is called Jeshurun, meaning “the upright one.”

Those who truly belong to Israel in the spiritual sense are people without deceit.

God acknowledges those who serve him.

He helps them through their difficulties and supports them in their service.

Water represents the Holy Spirit.

Just as water refreshes, cleanses and makes the earth fruitful, the Spirit brings spiritual renewal, purification and fruitfulness to the soul.

The gift of the Holy Spirit is the great blessing whose abundant outpouring God reserved for the latter days.

Where God gives his Spirit, he also gives every other blessing needed.

Through this gift, the church will grow greatly and spread into distant regions.

Is there any other Rock or Protector who can defend God's people?

No other being could announce in advance the things God had revealed through his prophets.

Divine predictions were ordered just as surely as God's purposes.

Who can compare with Israel's Redeemer and King?

The emptiness of handmade gods (verses 9–20)

The description of image-making exposes the foolishness of idolatry.

A person takes a piece of wood and uses part of it as fuel.

From what remains, the same person makes an image, bows before it and begs it for deliverance.

Human beings dishonor God when they attempt to represent him as a human image.

Satan blinds unbelievers' eyes, leading them into absurd reasoning about religion.

People who seek lasting happiness in worldly possessions, unbelief, superstition or any other false system are feeding on ashes.

Pride, love of sin and departure from God deceive the heart and lead it away from his truth and worship.

While our desires remain corrupt, we cling to a lie as though it were our most valuable treasure.

Are our hearts absorbed in the world's wealth and pleasures?

Those things will ultimately betray our hope.

If we depend on an outward religious profession or on our own actions to save us, we deceive ourselves as surely as idolaters do.

Learning to suspect our own self-deception is the first step toward deliverance from it.

Anyone concerned for the soul should examine the conscience and ask:

“Is there not a lie in my right hand?”

The Lord calls his redeemed people home (verses 21–28)

Return to me.

People who have wandered away from God, like the ancient Jews, should hurry to return to him.

The redemption Christ accomplished for us gives us reason to expect every blessing we need from him.

Our sins resemble a thick cloud hanging between heaven and earth.

Sin separates us from God and threatens a storm of divine judgment.

When the Lord pardons sin, he wipes away and disperses that cloud.

The way to heaven is opened again.

The Sun of Righteousness scatters the cloud completely.

Comfort after pardon resembles sunshine following darkness and rain.

Israel need not despair.

Nothing is too difficult for the God who made everything and can direct every creature to accomplish his purpose.

Once people know Christ, every other kind of knowledge seems insignificant in comparison with knowing him.

God turns the schemes of Christ's enemies into foolishness and catches them in their own cleverness.

The accurate fulfillment of Scripture's prophecies confirms its truth and its divine origin.

God announced particular favors for the people who would later be exiled long before their captivity took place.

Their return would face enormous obstacles, but divine power would remove them.

God knew the person who would deliver them and revealed his name so that, when his people heard of him, they would recognize that deliverance was drawing near.

For a great person, the highest honor is to serve as an instrument of divine kindness toward God's people.

Even people who seek only their own interests fulfill God's secret purposes.

And there is a greater Shepherd than Cyrus, who carries out his Father's will until his entire work is accomplished.

[Isa.44.21-Isa.44.28]

The work of redemption wrought for us by Christ, encourages to hope for all blessings from him. Our transgressions and our sins are as a thick cloud between heaven and earth: sins separate between us and God; they threaten a storm of wrath. When God pardons sin, he blots out, he dispels this cloud, this thick cloud, so that the way to heaven is open again. The cloud is scattered by the Sun of righteousness; it is quite gone. The particular favours God designed for his people in captivity, were foretold here, long before they went into captivity. Very great difficulties would be in the way of their deliverance; but it is promised that by Divine power they should all be removed. God knew who should be the Deliverer of his people; and let his church know it, that when they heard such a name talked of, they might know their redemption drew nigh. It is the greatest honour of the greatest men, to be employed as instruments of the Divine favour to his people. In things wherein men serve themselves, and look no further, God makes them do all his pleasure. And a nobler Shepherd than Cyrus does his Father's will, till his work is fully completed.

Cyrus is appointed to deliver Israel (verses 1–4)

Cyrus is called God's anointed, because God's counsel had appointed and equipped him for an important service.

Henry recounts how, on the night Cyrus entered Babylon, the gates leading from the city to the river were left open and his army advanced through the emptied river channel.

The Lord went before Cyrus, opening the cities he besieged.

He also gave him treasures concealed in secret places.

The true God was unknown to Cyrus, yet God had known him in advance and had called him by name.

The precise fulfillment of these words should have taught Cyrus that Jehovah was the only true God and that he had prospered for Israel's sake.

Through all the changes of states and kingdoms, the Lord works for the good of his church.

The sovereign Lord cannot be challenged (verses 5–10)

There is no God besides Jehovah.

Nothing takes place outside his sovereign rule.

He creates peace, here referring to every kind of good, and he brings evil in the sense of punishment or calamity, not moral evil or sin.

God is the source of everything true, holy, good and happy.

Error, moral evil and misery came into the world through the willful apostasy of his creatures, under his permission.

Yet he restrains and overrules those evils for his righteous purposes.

This teaching comforted those longing earnestly for Israel's deliverance while waiting patiently for it.

But it chiefly points, in Henry's explanation, to the redemption of sinners through God's Son and to the Spirit's outpouring that makes the gospel fruitful.

We must not expect salvation without righteousness: the Lord has brought both together.

Oppressors must not resist God's purposes for his people.

And oppressed believers should not murmur as though God treated them unkindly.

Human beings are like earthen pots and broken pieces of pottery, made more broken still through conflict with one another.

It is as foolish for us to quarrel with God as for clay to accuse the potter.

Turn God's promises into prayers.

Ask him to cause salvation and righteousness to abound among us.

Rest assured that the Judge of all the earth will do right.

God's people will be established (verses 11–19)

Believers may ask God for what they need.

If a request is truly for their good, he will not withhold what is best.

Yet how often people call God to account, as though he owed them explanations for every part of his conduct!

Trust the name of the Lord.

Rest upon the promises of his covenant and build hope upon them.

Trust Jesus Christ, the Lord our Righteousness, and lean upon God as our God through the Mediator.

But presumptuous sinners are warned against placing confidence in themselves.

Their supposed merit and strength appear to them like warmth and light.

Earthly comforts are mere sparks: they burn briefly and then disappear.

Yet worldly people try to warm themselves by them while enjoying the pride and pleasures of their passing light.

Those who make the world their comfort and their own righteousness their confidence will finally encounter bitterness.

A godly person's path may be dark now, but it leads to peace and everlasting light.

An ungodly person's path may appear pleasant, but it ends in lasting darkness.
classic_reading:
[Isa.50.1-Isa.50.3]
Chapter 50
The rejection of the Jews. ( [Isa.50.1-Isa.50.3] Is. 50:1-3) The sufferings and exaltation of the Messiah. ( [Isa.50.4-Isa.50.9] Is. 50:4-9) Consolation to the believer, and warning to the unbeliever. ( [Isa.50.10] Is. 50:10, [Isa.50.11] 11)
Verses 1-3 Those who have professed to be people of God, and seem to be dealt severely with, are apt to complain, as if God had been hard with them. Here is an answer for such murmurings; God never deprived any of their advantages, except for their sins. The Jews were sent into Babylon for their idolatry, a sin which broke the covenant; and they were at last rejected for crucifying the Lord of glory. God called on them to leave their sins, and prevent their own ruin. Last of all, the Son came to his own, but his own received him not. When God calls men to happiness, and they will not answer, they are justly left to be miserable. To silence doubts concerning his power, proofs of it are given. The wonders which attended his sufferings and death, proclaimed that he was the Son of God, Matt. 27:54.
[Isa.50.4-Isa.50.9]
Verses 4-9 As Jesus was God and man in one person, we find him sometimes speaking, or spoken of, as the Lord God; at other times, as man and the servant of Jehovah. He was to declare the truths which comfort the broken, contrite heart, those weary of sin, harassed with afflictions. And as the Holy Spirit was upon him, that he might speak as never man spake; so the same Divine influence daily wakened him to pray, to preach the gospel, and to receive and deliver the whole will of the Father. The Father justified the Son when he accepted the satisfaction he made for the sin of man. Christ speaks in the name of all believers. Who dares to be an enemy to those unto whom he is a Friend? or who will contend with those whom he is an Advocate? Thus St. Paul applies it, Rom. 8:33.
[Isa.50.10-Isa.50.11]
Verse 10 ,11 A child of God is afraid of incurring his displeasure. This grace usually appears most in believers when in darkness, when other graces appear not. Those that truly fear God, obey the voice of Christ. A sincere servant of God may for a long time be without views of eternal happiness. What is likely to be an effectual cure in this sad case? Let him trust in the name of the Lord; and let him stay himself upon the promises of the covenant, and build his hopes on them. Let him trust in Christ, trust in that name of his, The Lord our Righteousness; stay himself upon God as his God, in and through a Mediator. Presuming sinners are warned not to trust in themselves. Their own merit and sufficiency are light and heat to them. Creature-comforts are as sparks, short-lived, and soon gone; yet the children of this world, while they last, seek to warm themselves by them, and walk with pride and pleasure in the light of them. Those that make the world their comfort, and their own righteousness their confidence, will certainly meet with bitterness in the end. A godly man's way may be dark, but his end shall be peace and everlasting light. A wicked man's way may be pleasant, but his end and abode for ever will be utter darkness.
